title: Loadgen warmup impact analysis and seed hygiene
body:
Purpose:
This note documents a focused set of experiments and practical guidance about warmup behavior in our throughput benchmarking harness. The goal is pragmatic: reduce run-to-run variance, avoid false regressions, and produce a repeatable steady-state throughput number that correlates with production tail behavior.

Executive summary / TL;DR:
- Warmup length is highly sensitive to sequence-length distribution and KV-cache policy; short sequences (<=64 tokens) typically hit steady throughput after ~30s, long sequences (>512) can take 3–5 minutes to stabilize.
- RNG seed hygiene (per-client RNG vs global RNG) accounts for ~6–12% variance in synthetic request mixes with randomized prompts. Use per-worker deterministic seeds saved with the run metadata.
- Recommended default harness policy: 2-phase warmup (priming + confirmation), where priming uses a higher arrival rate for a short duration to populate caches followed by a confirmation window at target arrival rate to validate stability. Typical parameters: priming 60s @ 1.5x target RPS, confirmation 90s @ target RPS, stability threshold 2.5% p95 change.
- Always capture token-level and KV-cache hit metrics and include them in run artifacts; absence of cache metrics is a common source of irreproducibility.

Experimental setup (short):
- Hardware: 4x A100-80GB, single model per GPU, no other tenant load.
- Model variants: base FP16 and q4_0 quantized variant.
- Workloads: two canonical mixes used in all experiments: 
  * short-chat: 75% seq<=64, 20% seq 65-256, 5% longer
  * long-tail: 40% seq<=64, 40% 256-512, 20% >512
- Load generator: benchctl v0.9.1 (our internal runner), configured to emit Poisson arrivals with optional microburst mode.
- Metrics captured: tokens/sec, requests/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, GPU util, GPU memory, KV cache hits/misses, kernel occupancy, batching stats (avg batch size, batch freq).

Representative loadgen config snippets (YAML-like):
# priming phase
priming:
  duration_s: 60
  multiplier_of_target_rps: 1.5
  arrival_process: poisson
  rng_seed_policy: per_worker_deterministic

# confirmation phase
confirmation:
  duration_s: 90
  multiplier_of_target_rps: 1.0
  arrival_process: poisson
  measure_window_s: 30
  stability_threshold_pct: 2.5

# arrival mix
mixes:
  short_chat:
    distribution: ["<=64:0.75", "65-256:0.20", ">256:0.05"]
  long_tail:
    distribution: ["<=64:0.40", "256-512:0.40", ">512:0.20"]

Seed hygiene and determinism: practical rules
- Use explicit per-worker deterministic RNG seeds. benchctl supports "seed=run_id:worker_id" templating which yields reproducible interleavings across runs.
- Do NOT rely on a single process-wide RNG for the whole harness; that couples client scheduling and request content ordering across workers and increases variance.
- Record the full seed map in the run metadata JSON (benchctl emits seed_map.json). Attach that to the benchmark artifact.

Warmup behavior observations and heuristics (detailed):
1) KV cache priming dominates long-sequence stabilization. If your model implements KV caching on the server side, a single long sequence can change internal memory layout and subsequent kernel selection; realistic warmup must include representative long context requests.
2) Batching ramps: continuous batching behavior introduces an effective delay while kernels ramp up to an average batch occupancy. For small batches, variance in client inter-arrival will produce measurement noise; prefer Poisson arrivals with a small CV (0.8–1.2) for deterministic results.
3) GPU kernel path selection: transitions between kernel variants (e.g., 8-bit matmul vs 16-bit) happen when sequence length/occupancy crosses thresholds; include sequences that straddle these thresholds in the priming mix.

Repeatability checklist (run before marking a result as authoritative):
- [ ] benchctl version recorded in run meta
- [ ] seed_map.json present and attached
- [ ] pipeline: priming + confirmation phases used
- [ ] GPU thermals within 5C of baseline
- [ ] No other user workloads on node (node isolation verified)
- [ ] KV cache hit rate and avg batch size reported
- [ ] p95 change during confirmation window < stability_threshold_pct

Noise quantification and how to report it:
- Report median and 95% CI for tokens/sec over the confirmation windows across N=5 independent runs (different run_id and different seed maps). We use bootstrap CI with 1000 resamples.
- If the coefficient of variation (std/mean) across runs > 3% for tokens/sec, the workload is considered high-variance and requires extended confirmation (double confirmation duration) or larger N.

Example observed numbers (short_chat, target 20 RPS):
- run A (no seed hygiene): tokens/sec 18500, p95 120 ms
- run B (per-worker seeds, priming+confirm): tokens/sec 19700, p95 95 ms
- variance reduction observed: ~8% improvement in mean throughput and 40% reduction in p95 spread across runs when using recommended harness.

Common pitfalls and postmortem notes from past outages:
- False negative regressions were caused by missing KV cache priming in the benchmark harness when comparing q4 quantized model to FP16 (the quantized model's kernel path warmed slower).
- Using very short confirmation windows (<30s) led to flip-flops in release gate checks; increased to >=90s fixed most cases.
- Build artifacts (different BLAS/cuDNN versions) produced subtle throughput changes; always pin runtime software and include git/imagenet hashes in run meta.

Practical quick commands (examples):
# start a run with explicit run id and seed policy
benchctl run --run-id=2025-10-02-shortchat-v2 --config=short_chat.yaml --seed-policy=per_worker_deterministic

# collect artifacts and upload
benchctl collect --run-id=2025-10-02-shortchat-v2 --output ./artifacts/2025-10-02-shortchat-v2.zip

Run artifact contents we expect to persist: 
- metrics.csv (1s granularity)
- seed_map.json
- hw_snapshot.json (gpu temps, driver, kernel versions)
- batching_stats.json
- raw log (benchctl.log)

Open items / experiments to follow up:
- Test microburst priming vs sustained mild overprovisioning: measure whether a short high-rate spike provides better long-term stabilization than an extended 1.2x priming.
- Quantify the relationship between model kv eviction policy and stabilization time (models with smaller kv capacity may re-evict frequently under mixed sequences).
- Investigate automated adaptive confirmation duration: algorithmically lengthen confirmation when p95 drift > threshold during confirmation.

Actionable recommendations (short):
- Update benchctl default workflow to instrument and require priming + confirmation phases (see linked PR).
- Make seed_map.json mandatory artifact and bake into CI acceptance criteria for throughput checks.
- In release notes for model swaps, include expected stabilization time and recommended warmup profile.

Appendix: quick reference table (recommended defaults)
- priming duration: 60s
- priming multiplier: 1.25–1.5x target RPS
- confirmation duration: 90s (min 30s measure window)
- runs per data point: >=5
- low-variance threshold (tokens/sec): CV < 0.03

If you run into surprising instability please ping #eng-serving-runtime and attach the run artifact zip.

Notes to self / scratch:
- Try priming with model-swapped weights to measure kernel selection hysteresis.
- Add a small client-side jitter generator to avoid pathological alignment when multiple bench runners are co-located.

(End)
